'''Lao Genevra Simons''' (1870–1949) also referred to as '''Lao G. Simons''', was an American mathematician, writer, and [[history of mathematics|historian of mathematics]] known for her influential book ''Fabre and Mathematics and Other Essays''. Simons was   head of the mathematics department at [[Hunter College]] in New York.

== Life ==
Lao Genevra Simons was born on March 25, 1870, in [[San Jose, California]]. When Simons was six months old, her family moved east to New Jersey.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|date=1950|title=Obituaries|journal=Isis|publisher=The University of Chicago Press on behalf of The History of Science Society|volume=41|issue=2|pages=202|jstor=227193|issn=0021-1753}}</ref>

Upon retiring from Hunter College, Simons founded a $1000 scholarship for the university named after the mathematics honour society, Pi Mu Epsilon. A second graduate scholarship was created in her name, funded by friends, alumnae, and admirers, in the same year.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://library.hunter.cuny.edu/old/sites/default/files/pdf/archive_articles/in_memoriam-dr._lao_generva_simons.pdf|title=IN MEMORIAM|last1=Landers|first1=Mary K.|author-link=Mary Landers|last2=McLaughlin|first2=Isabel C.|date=1950|website=Hunter College Archives|access-date=February 1, 2020|last3=Eisele|first3=Carolyn|author-link3=Carolyn Eisele}}</ref>

Simons died on November 25, 1949, in [[Greenwich, Connecticut]], at age 79 of natural causes.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

=== Education ===
As a child, Simons attended school in New Jersey. She later obtained a teaching certificate from the [[Teachers College, Columbia University|College for the Training of Teachers]] at [[Columbia University]] and later studied astronomy and mathematics for a year at [[Vassar College]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/simons.htm|title=Lao Genevra Simons|last=Riddle|first=Larry|website=www.agnesscott.edu|access-date=2020-01-30}}</ref>

Simons earned a bachelor of science in 1908 from Columbia University; she attained a master’s degree and a Ph.D. also from Columbia in 1912 and 1924 respectively.<ref name=":1" /> Her Ph.D. was obtained with a major in education and a minor in mathematics. Simons' doctoral thesis was entitled ''Introduction of algebra into American schools in the eighteenth century''.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|date=1926|title=Notes|url=https://www.ams.org/journal-getitem?pii=S0002-9904-1926-04196-3|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=32|issue=2|pages=180|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1926-04196-3|issn=0002-9904|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Career ==
After obtaining her teaching certificate she taught at a preparatory school in Connecticut, then taught elementary school for a year in [[South Orange, New Jersey]].<ref name=":1" />

Simons was hired at a mathematics professor at Hunter College in 1895. This appointment did not require a bachelor's degree, which Simons did not have at the time of her initial hiring. In 1916, she became an assistant professor and in 1925, she became an associate professor. Simons would later be promoted to professor and head of the mathematics department at Hunter College in 1928.<ref name=":2" />

At Hunter College, Simons was Chairman of Student Activities from 1934, when the committee was initially founded, until 1940.<ref name=":2" /> Simons taught elective courses in mathematics, including advanced classes in [[pure mathematics]] and classes in the history of mathematics, in addition to required classes; Simons was one of the first mathematics professors at Hunter to do so. Simons worked at Hunter College until her retirement in 1940.<ref name=":1" />

Simons was elected a member of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in September 1923.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Richardson|first=R. G. D.|author-link=Roland Richardson|date=1923|title=The thirtieth summer meeting of the American Mathematical Society|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183485741|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|volume=29|issue=10|pages=433–444|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1923-03790-7|via=Project Euclid|doi-access=free}}</ref> Simons was also a member of the Council of The History of Science Society.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brasch|first=Frederick E.|author-link=Frederick Edward Brasch|date=1928|title=Proceedings of the Council Meeting of the History of Science Society|journal=Isis|volume=10|issue=2|pages=338–339|doi=10.1086/346326|jstor=224502|s2cid=144235068|issn=0021-1753}}</ref> As part of the Council, Simons was part of the committee on arrangements for the meeting and exhibition commemorating the bi-centenary of the death of Sir Isaac Newton.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brasch|first=Frederick E.|date=1928|title=Report of the Meeting and Exhibition Commemorating the Bi-Centenary of the Death of Sir Isaac Newton|journal=Isis|volume=10|issue=2|pages=334|doi=10.1086/346325|jstor=224501|s2cid=143954684|issn=0021-1753}}</ref>

Simons wrote articles about math history for ''[[Scripta Mathematica]]'', ''The Mathematics Teacher'', and the ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]''. Simons was an associate editor for Scripta Mathematica,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Slaught|first=H. E.|date=1933|title=Scripta Mathematica|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=40|issue=4|pages=231|jstor=2302179|issn=0002-9890}}</ref> and from 1932, the founding year of the journal, to 1949 she served as its Book Review Editor.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

== Works ==

* ''Introduction of algebra into American schools in the eighteenth century''  (1924), doctoral thesis<ref name=":3" />
** Simons said of this publication that its purpose was "to show that algebra entered into the American education of the eighteenth century, and to show further that we must seek some other reason for its presence than a practical need for it."<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1925|title=Notes and News|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=32|issue=5|pages=270|jstor=2299216|issn=0002-9890}}</ref>
* “[https://www.jstor.org/stable/2298974 Algebra at Harvard College in 1730]” (1925) in The American Mathematical Monthly, Vol. 32, No. 2, pp.&nbsp;63–70
* ''[http://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/history/simons/index.html Bibliography of Early American Textbooks on Algebra]'' (1936)
** A summary and description of America algebra textbooks published through 1850<ref name=":1" />
* ''[http://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/history/fabre/index.html Fabre and Mathematics and Other Essays]'' (1939)
** The book contained three previously published essays: "Fabre and Mathematics", "The Influence of French Mathematicians at the End of the Eighteenth Century upon the Teaching of Mathematics in American Colleges", and "Short Stories in Colonial Geometry"<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Daniells|first=Marian E.|date=1939|title=Review of Fabre and Mathematics and Other Essays|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=46|issue=10|pages=646–647|doi=10.2307/2303210|jstor=2303210|issn=0002-9890}}</ref>
** The only new essay published in ''Fabre and Mathematics'' was "The Interest of Alexander von Humboldt in Mathematics"<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Daniells|first=Marian E.|date=1939|title=Review of Fabre and Mathematics and Other Essays|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=46|issue=10|pages=646|doi=10.2307/2303210|jstor=2303210|issn=0002-9890}}</ref>
